subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO PRESENTATION OF BUDGET ON FRIDAY, MAY 1

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): In reply to the question asked yesterday by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), I hope to be able to present the budget on Friday of this week.
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) if his attention has been drawn to a circular letter signed by J. S. Norris, president of the Beauharnois corporation, and dated at Montreal, March 20, 1936, in which appears this statement:
The project became the subject of entirely unwarranted and purely political attacks in the federal parliament of Canada early in 1931.
In view of the verdict of parliament given at that time, what steps will the government take to see that parliament is protected from unwarranted statements and attacks of this description which will mislead the bondholders who are meeting to consider the matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons is master of its own house. I prefer to leave it to the House of Commons to say what shall be done.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I wonder if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Coldwell) would let me see that circular? If I understood him aright I think the matter is more serious than one which could be left merely to the House of Commons. This statement challenges this house in a very peculiar way. I quote from the letter as follows:
The project became the subject of entirely unwarranted and purely political attacks in the federal parliament of Canada early in 1931.
The effects of these political attacks upon the enterprise were extremely serious and far-reaching. They resulted:
In the cancellation of the approval previously obtained under the Navigable Waters Protection Act;
In the reestablishment by special act of the federal parliament of a basis of federal approval subject to new and undisclosed conditions;
In Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company being forced to convey to the crown over 9,000 arpents of land (representing a cash outlay of over $1,800,000) upon which works had already been constructed by the company costing upwards of $15,000,000. The company received no compensation whatever for these works other than an easement to use the property, so conveyed, for power purposes;
In the federal government being forced to assist in the temporary financing of the enterprise by guaranteeing, against ultimate loss, bank advances aggregating nearly $16,000,000 made to prevent the collapse of the enterprise;
And finally, in the reorganization of Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited and Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, in June, 1933.
I have not had any previous conversation with the hon. gentleman who has brought this matter to the attention of the house, but on listening to him it struck me that this is a serious reflection upon the privileges of parliament. I think perhaps this house has been rather careless in the assertion of its privileges, though in one or two instances it has done so. As soon as the hon. gentleman began to speak I sent for Sir Austen Chamberlain's book, Down the Years, and I would direct the attention of the house to this one reminiscence as given, beginning at page 70, because Sir Austen Chamberlain refers to a matter of this kind with a good deal of care:
Parliament was dissolved only four months later and my first House of Commons has left only one abiding impression on my mind. It is of the greatness of Mr. Speaker Peel. The house has had many great Speakers, but I doubt whether in its long history it has ever had a greater than Arthur Wellesley Peel. Others have served it faithfully and many of them with great distinction, but Speaker Peel dominated it. In the opinion not only of one like myself who was still a young member when he retired, but of older men who had been present at his first election, he stood in a class by himself, over-topping his predecessors, never equalled even by the most successful and respected of his successors. He had a natural dignity and a formal but genuine courtesy which well became the occupant of the chair, and, besides, a dramatic gift which in great moments raised him far above his fellow members that the whole house trembled at his rebuke. At such times his stature seemed to grow before our eyes, his deep resonant voice dominated the tumult and he appeared as the living embodiment of centuries of parliamentary tradition.
One such moment occurred in the closing days of the parliament of 1892. A select committee of the house had been inquiring into
Beauharnois Power Corporation

the hours of work of railway servants, and among the witnesses who had given evidence before it was the stationmaster of some small station on the Cambrian railway. He had subsequently been called before three of the directors and the general manager of the company and dismissed, nominally for some irregularities in his accounts but really, as was obvious from the questions put to him by the directors, on account of the evidence which he had given before the select committee. The committee, of which Sir Michael Hicks Beach was chairman, took evidence as to what had passed and made a special report to the house on the case as a breach of privilege. Of the three directors involved one, Sir John Maclure, was an old and much-liked member of the house. A day was fixed for the discussion and an order was made by the house that the honourable member for Stratford should attend in his place and that his co-directors and the general manager should appear at the bar. They were asked if they had anything to say and Sir John Maclure offered an apology with which the others associated themselves. They were then ordered to withdraw while their case was considered, and Hicks Beach moved:	"That this house while recognizing
that they had expressed their unqualified regret for having unintentionally infringed any of its rules and privileges is of opinion that they have committed a breach of privilege . .. and that they be called in and admonished by Mr. Speaker."
This seemed a rather lame conclusion and there was a good deal of sympathy -with the proposal made by T. P. O'Connor to add that the house would not consider that they had purged their contempt till they had reinstated the discharged man. Efforts were made privately to get them to do this, or at least to compensate him, but they remained obdurate. Hicks Beach's resolution was supported by Mr. Gladstone, but his advice was rejected by the great majority of his followers whose zeal for the injured man was perhaps stimulated by the value of the railway vote at the general election which was known to be imminent. A long, wrangling discussion followed and it was not till midnight that a division was taken and Hicks Beach's resolution carried.
Then the directors were once more called in. Sir John Maclure evidently felt his position acutely^ but the other three appeared at the bar defiantly and almost jauntily. They had successfully resisted the desire of many members, not confined to one side of the house, that they should compensate the man, and now they were to have what schoolboys call a "pi-jaw" from the Speaker-that was all the House of Commons could do to them.
Mr. Speaker Peel spoke for less than ten minutes. "I would have you to know-each and all of you gentlemen-that though the privileges of this house are not be put into operation on any light or trivial occasion ... yet a privilege of this house is no unreal, shadowy or unsubstantial thing; it is what the house clings to and what it is determined to maintain." And then after expatiating on the enormity of their particular offence, he declared "The house in its judgment and, I should add, in its mercy has decided that I should admonish you," and he proceeded to administer the admonition.
The bald words of what he said, recorded in Hansard, convey no idea of the devastating
{Mr. Bennett.]
effect of that short allocution. The men who had come to the bar so defiantly a few minutes earlier wilted under his admonition; beads of perspiration stood out on their foreheads and, when he dismissed them, they crept away like whipped hounds, while the rest of us shook ourselves like dogs coming out of the water and thanked heaven we had not been in the position of poor Maclure.
I do say that the statement sent- broadcast to the shareholders of this enterprise over the signature of Mr. J. S. Norris, president, is a distinct breach of the privileges of this house; and thus to reflect upon the action that was taken not only by the committee but by the House of Commons itself, ultimately by unanimous action, is something that should not be tolerated or permitted. Moreover, one at least of the statements is not correct, I refer to the paragraph indicating that all they had received was an easement to use the property, so conveyed, for power purposes. That is entirely beside the question and is not in any sense an adequate expression of what was received in compensation for the title being vested in the crown, and I cannot but think that it is the duty of the government to take cognizance of this matter, for the maintenance of the traditions and the honour of the house is in the keeping primarily of the government of the day; and possibly a committee should be set up for the purpose of investigating the matter, so that if there is found to have been a violation of the privileges of this house appropriate action may be taken.
These things seem trifling and perhaps they are; they seem to be matters that should be treated as a joke, of little importance; and yet the maintenance of the privileges of this house is fundamental if we are to maintain the supremacy of parliament itself. Parliament cannot retain the respect and esteem of the people if it permits itself to be attacked in the way in which it has been and men feel that because they occupy the position of members of the House of Commons they must be subject to this sort of criticism and attack upon their actions. The parliament at Westminster, even in the most turbulent days, has been very careful to preserve untarnished its honour and undimin-ish'ed the assertion of its rights, to maintain the privileges of parliament as such.
I think the hon. gentleman is to be thanked for bringing the matter to the attention of the house. I had seen reference to it in the newspapers but I had not seen this document in its entirety, although I had heard what the general- contents of it were. I suggest it warrants careful consideration on the part

Beauharnois Power Corporation
of the government and in particular of the Prime Minister. It might be that, inasmuch as there is little time now to consider it, in view of the record-and I think I have given the whole of the statement, as will appear in Hansard-the right hon. gentleman should take time to look into the matter and determine what should be the appropriate action in the circumstances with a view to maintaining the ancient privileges of parliament and its position in the country itself.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I must confess I have
been at a loss to know just what we have been discussing. We are on the orders of the day, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) 'having been for a long time in parliament and having for some years held the position of first minister, I did not think it proper to interrupt him or to call him to order. Certainly, however, I think he was decidedly out of order. If the subject under consideration is a question which affects the privileges of the house I suggest that in its consideration there ought at least to be an observance of the rules of the house on the part of all who are present.
First of all, speaking of the privileges and the rules of the house, may I say that it is customary, when an important question is going to be asked of the government on the orders of the day, for at least some intimation to be given in advance to the leader of the government or some member of it. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) asked the question which he did without having given previous intimation to me or, as far as I can gather, to any of my colleagues, with respect to the matter to which he was referring. He brought a document into the house, made some reference to it and asked me what the government was going to do about it. I am not the government-I differ in that respect perhaps from some others-and I like to have at least an opportunity of conferring with my colleagues before answering a question addressed to the government as such. I would have told the hon. member very frankly that such was my position if I had not thought that the answer which I gave was all-sufficient. To my amazement, I next find the leader of the opposition taking possession of the document, reading the whole of it for the purpose, as he says, of placing its contents on Hansard, giving his views with reference to the same, and then reading from some authority in alleged support of what he is saying. I have not, like the
leader of the opposition, come here armed with authorities purporting to support what I wish to say and of the point which I.am making. I think, however, there should be very little difficulty for any hon. member of the house to know where ample authorities may be found for what I have already expressed, namely that if the privileges of this house have been violated in any way it is open to any member of the house to bring the matter up and it is for the house itself to take such action as it may deem necessary and advisable. The House of Commons is the custodian of its own privileges; the government is not the custodian of the privileges of the House of Commons. Every hon. member has the same right as the Prime Minister in a matter of privilege, and no one knows it better than the leader of the opposition.
May I say one thing further with regard to the question which has been asked. Is it to be assumed that a citizen of this country is not to have the right to criticize the action of a government? AVhat is to become of freedom of expression in this country if every citizen is to be told that if he ventures to criticize anything which has been done by the parliament of Canada he is immediately to be brought to the bar of parliament to answer for it? That is not my view, at any rate, of the rights either of government or of citizenship.
I repeat that I had not seen the document to which reference has been made by the hon. member. It had not been brought to my attention. I knew nothing of its contents. He was careful, I suppose because it had some reference to Beauharnois, to seek to make a play with it, just as the leader of the opposition has sought to do.
That is unfair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But such things are easily understood by anybody. As far as the question asked is concerned I return to what I said at the beginning, that if any privilege of this house has been violated, hon. members may take the matter into their own hands and deal with it as they see fit. So far as the government is concerned it is going to sustain the right of free expression of opinion by the citizens of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-
Mr. Speaker-

of the first importance with regard to the privileges of this house, and I was raising the question of privilege; that is all.

Rising to a point of
order, I wish to say that an inference may be taken from the remarks of the right hon.

that I do not think my remarks are capable of that interpretation, but I am not surprised that my hon. friend supposed that some hon. members might well have thought so after listening to the leader of the opposition.

Experimental projects and large scale demonstrations therefrom, $214,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Before we begin the discussion of this item, Mr. Chairman, I should like just to say to you how pleased hon. members of this house are to see you again in the chair, restored, we trust, to your former health and strength.
I should like on behalf of those with whom I am associated to join with the right hon. Prime Minister in what he has just said.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
This item, which proposes to
provide $448,000 for expenditure upon projects already undertaken, covers expenditures that were provided for last year in connection with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. These expenditures cover, under the first item, experimental projects and large scale demonstrations therefrom in the amount of $214,000. This amount has to do with experiments that are being carried on at experimental stations throughout the southern part of Saskatchewan, the southern part of Alberta and the southwestern part of Manitoba, and provision for the distribution of grass seeds and other methods of demonstrating the use of some of the products that have been developed through experimentation. It also has to do with the promotion of strip farming and everything of that nature tending toward the better use of lands in the area of the provinces where we have had drought during the last five or six years.

I should like to ask the minister for a little further explanation of

Supply-Agriculture*-Rehabilitation
his reference to the distribution of seeds. Does the government supply the seeds free? Are the seeds grown on government land or on the lands of experimental farms, or are they grown on private farms, taken over by the government, and then distributed?
The experiments are carried on upon a number of demonstration farms that were selected last year.
Private farms?

Private farms, yes, the lands of which are rented under the same terms as ordinary demonstration farms, and rentals are paid for the use of these lands for demonstration purposes. Some of the grass seed, of course, will be used on those lands. Then there are associations composed of farmers who form themselves into an organization with a president, secretary and executive, who meet together from time to time and discuss ways and means of making use of grasses for different purposes. The government has purchased seed which it supplies through those associations to individual farmers to be used on plots of their own land in order to demonstrate the use of grasses in reestablishing these areas.
Is the seed supplied free?
Yes, it is free.

The second part of this item has to do with water development projects. I find it very difficult to get any conception of what that implies. There is a very large area that has suffered from drought and on which the distribution of water would be of inestimable benefit. There are large irrigation projects around Medicine Hat, for instance, but they involve very large structures and a tremendous amount of digging of ditches for distribution. I wonder if the minister would give a short explanation of what is being attempted under this item. Is this only demonstration work which will assist the individual farmer to carry on similar work on his own land, or does it affect whole districts which will benefit by the water dammed up?

A number of different methods are being followed in order to assist in this way. If the hon. member will look further down the page I think the works to which he is referring come under item 308, but this vote covers largely what are known as small dams and dugouts. Some two or three thousand of these have been proposed by persons residing in that part of the country extending from Crystal City in Manitoba
over a triangular area running right up to the foothills in Alberta. A number of those proposals were examined into by engineers last season; I think some six or seven hundred have been accepted as projects that should be carried through, and some two or three hundred others are under consideration at the moment. The money may be spent in two ways. Dams are placed across ravines in different parts of the territory, where it is feasible to do so, in order to provide a water supply, usually for three or more farmers. Sometimes it is done for a larger section of the community and in some instances it may be done on ranges operated for ranching purposes perhaps by individuals, but the work is spread over that whole area, some of 'which is wheat growing country, some mixed farming country and some purely ranching country. The dugouts are constructed largely throughout the wheat growing area, where it is impossible to have dams because of the nature of the country, and where it has not been possible to get water by the digging of wells. Dugouts are used particularly in the heavy soil country, assistance is given to the extent of three cents per yard for the earth that is moved, in connection with small dams. This money is to be spent to promote that sort of thing.
Then does the snow water fill these dugouts, and is that water ditched out extensively?

Under the plan that was set up last year engineers are sent out to advise the farmers whether they might obtain a water supply by digging a dugout. Of course that usually involves drainage from certain directions into the dugout. Sometimes there is the possibility of providing a run-off, but at- other times it is just like a slough, where the water collects and serves for the season.

I should like to ask the minister on what principle this vote is brought before this committee. In the first place agriculture is under concurrent jurisdiction between the dominion and the provinces. In the other provinces of Canada this question of rehabilitation is very largely a provincial matter. Why do not the prairie provinces themselves come forward with a scheme such as has been proposed by the minister? On the other hand, if it is proposed to carry on this work this year, why was not this item included in the main estimates? In the second place, Mr. Chairman, why is there not equality of treatment as between the prairie provinces and the maritime provinces, as between the farmers of the west and the

Supply-Agriculture-Rehabilitation
farmers of central Canada? Who is going to pay for all this? The cost will have to come out of the pockets of the workers in the central provinces, who have provincial legislatures looking after the question of agriculture.
Since this government came into power I have seen most radical departures from the principles laid down by the British North America Act. There has been the five-year census for the prairies and other things of that kind, and now we have agriculture. I admit that the farmers of the prairies are suffering, but their situation is no worse than that of the farmers of Ontario. I could show the minister farms in Ontario just as badly off as the farms of the other provinces. Since I have been in this house we have had royal commissions appointed to ascertain the situation with regard to various provinces of confederation. We have had royal commissions on maritime rights, prairie rights and Pacific rights, and the time is coming when the farmers of Ontario and Quebec, and the industrial workers who cannot get a dollar with which to save their homes from foreclosure, who have to pay the cost of all this sort of thing, will demand an investigation or survey too. The time is coming when Ontario and Quebec will have to ascertain what is their place under confederation as expressed by the British North America Act. The two central provinces must pay the cost of all this sort of thing, since they contribute eighty per cent of the cash taxes that are raised, and they are not going to remain forever hewers of wood and drawers of water for the rest of confederation. The principle of confederation in which I believe is expressed by the old Cornish battle cry, each for all and all for each. This item has also reference to farm rehabilitation. The question of rehabilitation was referred to the other day in Bill No. 14 and again in Bill No. 19, and I thought that matter had been handed over to a commission. We are a long way behind the times in rehabilitation in Canada when we consider what has been done for the farmers in Denmark and the United States, but are we going to have this matter handled by the minister, and another branch of the work under Bill 19 handled by Mr. Purvis?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would ask the hon.
member to confine himself to the item under discussion.

I accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but with all due deference I would point out that I am speaking of item 307 about the word in this item, "rehabilitation,"
(Mr. Church.]
which also appeared in Bill No. 19 the other day, in reference not only to industrial workers but also to agriculture. If we are to have farm rehabilitation for one province let us have it for all provinces; let us have equality of treatment so that not only t'he prairie provinces but the other provinces as well will get votes of money in the supplementary estimates.
Then this item 307 goes on to refer to experimental projects and large scale demonstrations. Only the other day we handed out six or seven million dollars for large scale demonstrations and now under this item we are asked to vote a further sum of $448,000. I am going	to	ask	the ministerto extend these handouts to the province of Ontario too, since this question of agriculture comes under the concurrent jurisdiction of the provinces and the dominion. H there is to be rehabilitation by Mr. Hepburn's administration in Ontario, the prairie prov-inches should pay as Ontario does for rehabilitation as well, and the construction of power projects. Look	at	the	hydro	waterpower project in Ontario; it was built at the expense of the province, and the dominion government did not contribute a nickel towards the cost. I admit that these other provinces have rights too, but there are provinces whose rights are forgotten. I refer to the two central provinces. If the Ontario and Quebec members	would	assert	theirrights they would have a royal commission to find the place of the	two	central	provinces in confederation, besides that of merely paying the debts.

All I would say in reply is that the caption which appears on the item, Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, pretty well indicates why the vote is here. That act was passed in 1935, the bill having been introduced by the then minister of agriculture. It provided for $750,000 last year, a million dollars this year and a million each year for the next three years following this; in other words it was a five year program. All that I have done as minister so far as this act and the amount of money provided by it is concerned is to cut it by a quarter of a million dollars. The provision made by the act is for a million dollars; I am providing only for the expenditure of $736,885.55 for these purposes in the first three votes under the heading of projects already undertaken, and under other projects in succeeding votes there is provided an amount of $559,556.69. These two amounts make a little more than one and a quarter million dollars. Two bills were passed last year, one providing a million dollars for

Supply-Agriculture-Rehabilitation
1936, and the other, I believe it was the Public Works Construction Act, which provided half a million for this and other purposes for the Department of Agriculture. Part of that half million dollars was spent last year; some of it still remains to be spent. I am asking the house to vote this year three quarters of a million under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and to provide for the expenditure of the remainder under the Public Works Construction Act of last session in connection with agriculture in the drought area of western Canada. These expenditures are being made only in the section where we have had drought during the last five or six years. I make that explanation not for the purpose of shirking any responsibility in connection with the vote, but simply in order to draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the amount was provided for by legislation of last year, and we are simply carrying out the purpose of that act.

In support of this proposed expenditure I believe the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) is labouring under a misapprehension. This is not a general policy for all the prairie provinces; as the minister has stated it just takes care of that part which has suffered so much from drought. I am sure the hon. member for Broadview, had he gone through that district, as I have done, and seen the ravages of the last five or six years of dry weather, would be one of the first to come to their relief. The fact that the previous government, of which he was a supporter, undertook this relief first, goes to prove what I say.
In regard to the dugouts to which reference has been made, I live in a district where we have to have them, and I may say to the hon. member for Broadview, whom I regard as a very good friend, that we have not asked the governments, either provincial or dominion, to reimburse the farmers making these dug-outs; they pay for it themselves. We are able to do that, but the people in the dried out areas are not, and unless we want to abandon them altogether we ought to be and I believe we are glad to offer any help we can to assist them through this period of stress.

I think the hon. gentleman was in error in making the statement about the million dollars. Section 8 of the act provides that:
For the purposes of this act the sum of $750,000 shall be appropriated and paid ... during the fiscal year 1935-36 and for each fiscal year for a further period of four years a sum not exceeding one million dollars per annum as may be necessary to continue and extend the work undertaken under this act.
Do I understand that the first two items amounting to 8448,000 are voted to discharge obligations already created?
Yes.
Then the 8750,000 of last year was spent in its entirety?
No.

Because the question of
the 8448,000 being part of the 8750,000 or in addition to the $750,000 becomes important.

The amount which is
being provided this year in the estimates, of the million dollars which the act provides we might have spent this year, is only $750,000; and that amount, together with a sum unexpended under the provision for 81,000,000 out of the Public Works Construction Act of last year, makes a total under these estimates of $1,296,442.24.

How much was
spent last year out of the $750,000?
I have not that information here at the moment. I could get it. It was about half of it.

Could the
minister give some information in respect to the $214,000 for experimental projects and large scale demonstrations? Does that include the establishment of demonstration farms?

Yes, it includes not
only the establishment of demonstration farms in the area but investigational work in connection with strip farming over considerable parts of the area. In southern Alberta, for example, strip farming has been carried on with considerable success for quite a number of years. There has been very little strip farming in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan, although there has been some. Under this expenditure there has been encouragement of strip farming in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan and the extension of it in Alberta and the use of it in part of Manitoba. The money spent in connection with it is for the sending out of men from the experimental farms to promote ithe spread of such projects; the actual work of distributing seed in connection with the sowing of grasses and everything of that kind comes out of this particular part of the vote.
It is not intended to purchase these farms, is it? They will be under lease?

No, there has been no purchasing of farms. The first project pre-

Have the legislatures of the prairie provinces taken over the rivers and streams and vested them in the provinces, in contradistinction to the rights of riparian owners and the general rights of the public in connection therewith?

That is a rather moot question. It has never been decided exactly what the relationship of the provinces to the streams is since the taking over of the natural resources. The whole matter with
regard to streams is under the same control in these provinces, or pretty much so, as elsewhere. Through that southern section of the three provinces, and more particularly in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, arrangements have to be entered into between this country and the United States with respect to the use made of streams for these purposes. That is all properly taken care of.
It is not quite correct to say that the rivers and streams in western Canada are in the same position as in other provinces.
Not exactly.

The Irrigation Act vested all waters in the crown in the right of the dominion, and whether they have been adequately transferred to the provinces has not yet been finally determined. In crown grants made by the crown in the right of the dominion there was a reservation to the crown of all waters, lakes, and areas covered by water, so that the property in the water is vested in the crown the same as precious minerals or metals, and the question of riparian owners is not one that arises at all.

What I have to say with respect to the answer given me by the Minister of Agriculture applies to the answer made by the leader of the opposition. He speaks of the crown, but the crown has a relationship to both the provinces and the dominion. In Nova Scotia, by the act of 1908, the legislature took over all rivers and streams, and this is within its rights. That is the very question that has been raised to-day in connection with Beauharnois. The premier of Quebec is reported to have said that so far as streams are concerned they are all within the province, and the leader of the opposition gave this opinion in this house at the last session in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth). That hon. gentleman asked him whether or not Beauharnois should come under public ownership and the answer he gave was that the rivers and streams were in the province and therefore the only thing the government had to do with when he was prime minister was the issuing of licences for the export of power. The right hon. gentleman also volunteered the statement that while there could not be public ownership so far as rivers and streams were concerned, he regretted very much that Sir Herbert Holt, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, was to-day in control of Beauharnois.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries):

speechtext:
Under this item may I
ask the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), in the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), to draw to the attention of the latter the remarks I am about to make. I wish to refer to the act passed in 1935 placing fishermen in the same category as farmers in respect to borrowing money, for the purpose of constructing new vessels and repairing old ones, and to some extent,, I think, obtaining fishing gear. Last year I drew the attention of the then government to the necessity of something being done along these lines. When the act came before the house in the last days of the session I was unavoidably absent. Had I been present I should have been able, I believe, to point out to the then government that the act in the form submitted to the house would not be effective in bringing about the result which was intended. The intentions were good, but the act could not be carried out. For instance, under it you cannot borrow money for, say the construction of new vessels except by giving a mortgage upon the real estate of the borrower. That does not help the general run of fishermen; ninety per cent of them cannot avail themselves of the act. Having a little real estate, and while they are engaged in fishing, their relatives at home being at some period of the year working on their farm properties, these fishermen feel that if they give a mortgage on their real estate, and their vessel is lost, the real estate would have to go and they would lose everything.
If the act were amended to provide for taking a bill of sale or a chattel mortgage upon the vessel, and the vessel itself, being new, were insured in a marine insurance company, in case of loss the government would receive the insurance and thus have money to loan back again to the fisherman who met with this disaster, and the money would go on being used from year to year in that way. My suggestion is that the act be amended so as to permit or oblige the fisherman to

Supply-Fisheries
give a chattel mortgage or bill of sale to the federal government on a vessel to be constructed under this act or under aid from the government. If it were found difficult to insure these vessels under marine insurance, the government would be in a position to require the companies to adopt some plan by which this insurance could be effected. Some difficulty arose two years ago in connection with insuring farm property. When a farmer borrowed money under the old act he had to insure the property up to at least the amount of the sum borrowed. Some of the insurance companies, the moment that he was in a position to borrow money from the government, con celled the insurance they had. I brought that matter two years ago to the attention of the finance department, and the then minister, Mr. Rhodes, undertook to make arrangements with the various insurance companies whereby, if that practice prevailed, it should cease. If the government can take means to see that the farmer is properly protected, the same thing can be done by way of aid to the fisherman, if it should be found difficult to obtain marine insurance. I would therefore request that the Minister of Fisheries draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to this matter and see whether some amendment cannot be adopted by which the act of 1935 will be made more workable.
The reason I stress that point is this: Outside one county in Nova Scotia, I represent the county in which there is the largest fishing fleet in the maritime provinces. To-day from 275 to 325 of a fleet leave our coasts on a Monday morning and return on the following Saturday night after spending the whole week fishing. Owing to the depressed condition of the codfish market during the last four or five years, particularly during the last two years and more especially since the imposition of sanctions against Italy completely shut off our market in that country for salt dried cod, the owners and crews of these vessels have not earned enough to keep the boats in repair. This year quite a number of these vessels will remain at the docks and will not be put to sea. It may be that during the last four or five years they have not been kept in repair and have become unseaworthy, while others need to be replaced by new vessels. Under this act that cannot be done, for the reasons I have already mentioned.
I believe the government should come to the assistance of these fishermen just as assistance has been given to farmers generally throughout the country. I heartily approve and support the giving of assistance to farmers; I think this will work out fairly
well, with a few slight changes, but if the government do not come to the aid of the fishermen then what is perhaps the most important industry in the maritime provinces will gradually disappear and many of our fishermen will have to give up their calling and look to the government for direct relief. It would pay the government to spend money in this way instead of giving direct relief to the fishermen,. They do not want relief; they want an opportunity to earn a living, as they have done in the past. They risk their lives on the deep sea in pursuit of their calling. Their industry, in common with other industries, has been hit by the depression, and they are not able to carry on as they have done in the past. This afternoon I listened with a great deal of interest to all that was said in support of the relief which is to be given in the stricken areas of the prairie provinces. I hold up both hands in support of what has been done in the past andi what is intended for the future. At the same time, however, we have misery and distress in the maritimes. What wheat is to our western farmers the fishing industry is to us in the maritimes, and we have a perfect right to expect from governments, both provincial and federal, that aid to which we are entitled in order to enable our people to carry on until this depression passes by. I am glad that by means of this vote a step has been taken in the direction of doing something for our fishermen. I consider the amount fairly small, but I approve the principle of doing something, through a vote of parliament, to come to the aid of our men.
Let me say to the Minister of Fisheries, however, that in whatever arrangements are made with the provincial government he and his department should not lose any of the supervision which should be retained over the-expenditure of the money. I contend that if we give money to the provincial governments in order to aid the fishermen the federal Department of Fisheries should have supervision over the expenditure of the money. I think some officials, either from Ottawa or from outside, should be appointed to see that all arrangements for the distribution and expenditure of this money in each of the maritime provinces, and in fact in any province where this money may be expended, are carried out properly. I hope the suggestions I have made to the minister concerning loans to fishermen for the construction and rehabilitation of vessels will be taken under serious consideration.

I have no objection to this particular amount of $300,000 which is to be

Supply-Fisheries
spent, in cooperation with the provinces, for the assistance of needy fishermen. Last session there was introduced by the late government a fisherman's protection bill which was a step in the direction of giving protection to these needy men so that they would not lose their homes, nets, boats and other property; it was an extension of the farm loan principle to the fisheries of this country. I contended then, as I contend now, however, that this protection should be extended to fishermen in all the provinces to the head of the lakes instead of just to those in the maritime provinces. I say that it should extend to the fishermen on the great lakes.
To-day we are giving protection to both farmers and fishermen, and quite rightly so. I agree with everything that has been said by the former Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) as to the situation of these poor people, both in the maritime provinces and on the great lakes. They are suffering many hardships to-day, but since the government have given protection to farmers and fishermen I want to ask them this question: Are you or are you not going to extend this same principle of protection to the industrial workers of this country, who are losing their homes through foreclosure and who are being put out on the street? These are skilled mechanics, artisans, carpenters, bricklayers and that class of people, who make up fifty-three per cent of the workers of the dominion. Are you going to extend this principle of protection to all the people all the time and not some of the people some of the time? The Minister of Labour said he would study that question.

Why make a football of the needy industrial workers while you give relief to fishermen and farmers? When will some vote appear in the supplementary estimates making a grant in behalf of the industrial workers? There is nothing
at all in the main estimates; not one dollar is voted for the needy industrial worker. I have no abjection to this vote. I hope it will pass, but I think we should have some statement of policy on behalf of the government as to whether or not they are going to extend this vote or to do anything for these industrial workers.

With all due respect, Mr. Chairman, item 314 says "to aid." What does "to aid" mean?
To aid, in cooperation with provincial governments concerned, in reestablishment of needy fishermen.
That is a protectionist statement and vote. I know the rules. The discussion is relevant. You must believe in protection yourself, sometimes, Mr. Chairman. This is advanced piotection, something never done before by this parliament. These matters come under property and civil rights and are in the jurisdiction of the provinces. This relief is going beyond that; this goes much further than the relief measures; this is going to give these people something in addition. No doubt needy fishermen need some new equipment, boats and that kind of thing, as set out in the bill before parliament last session. I did not object to that measure, but I think the government should now come along with relief for the needy industrialists who have been knocking at the door of parliament. They are on relief; all they can get is a hand-out of a few loaves of bread. They are entitled to the very same protection as are other workers. I have expressed that opinion before and I am going to express it at every opportunity I get because I believe that fifty per cent of the workers of this country are entitled to some form of protection the same as are those engaged in fisheries and agriculture. We have protection for some and not for others; if you are going to protect some people who are needy let us have this protection for all the people of Canada all the time who are in need and losing their houses, their businesses and all that kind of thing.

At an earlier stage of this session I complimented the Minister of Fisheries upon having come to the province of Nova Scotia to look into the needs and the distress of our people there in connection wdth the fishing industry. I also complimented the Minister of Railways and Marine upon his visit to us, and to him we look for future results. But to-day, when I look at the estimates brought down by the Minister of Fisheries I confess that I am absolutely disappointed. I thought of the fishing industry along the coast of Nova Scotia and
along the shores of the great province of New Brunswick, to which the former Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) has referred, an industry which is so hazardous in contradistinction to the fishing industry on the Pacific ocean, for on the Pacific they have the lovely sunshine and the smooth waters as against the terrific gales, the heavy seas and the awful chances taken by our fishermen on the Atlantic. If bon. members of this committee will look through the newspapers during the last month they will find that some thirty-five fishermen along the coast of Nova Scotia lost their lives in trying to pursue their industry in order that they might have a bite to eat in their homes for their children and themselves.
To-day the fisherman sets his nets or his traps on that coast, and what becomes of them? He looks out from his doorway on a rock-ribbed coast, and finds that these things with which he has to earn his livelihood are absolutely gone. We have had here this afternoon the estimates in reference to our middle west, the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. To these votes I take no exception. When provision is made by the minister for agricultural development and the removal of people from one set of lands to another in order that they may make a livelihood, no objection is raised by us. But, Mr. Chairman, there is only one of two places on which the fisherman can plant his foot; he can plant it either on the granite rock or in the Atlantic ocean. I would ask the Minister of Fisheries if he is at liberty to say what agreement he has entered into with the government of the province of Nova Scotia from which I come. As to the other provinces, hon. gentlemen here can ask that question for themselves. I come from the county of Halifax which extends along the coast from Ecum Secum to Hubbard's cove, 200 miles, and the people along that shore depend absolutely for their living, the maintenance of their families and the education of their children-and I was going to say some amusement, but I am afraid they get little of that-upon the fisheries. Along that coast, and particularly on the westerly side of Halifax harbour to Shad bay and the various districts as far as Hubbard's cove, the children have had to remain in bed to keep warm because their parents had not money to buy coal-and there are only granite rocks; there are no trees to cut down to give them warmth-let alone shoes for their children to wear to school. I support the government of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and in that
Supply-Fisheries

government I support the Minister of Fisheries, but when I see the miniature estimate brought down to help the fisheries I am not pleased. Undoubtedly the vote in the estimates is to cover expenditures in all provinces where fishing is an industry. I speak my mind because I thought that after the visit of the Minister of Fisheries to the maritime provinces there would have been an opportunity to discuss with him, this great problem and the attitude of the government thereon. I should have thought the opportunity would be given before the estimate was placed before the committee.
Already I have pointed out, in a communication addressed to the government, that I believe this year a bonus should be given to fishermen, not only to those in Nova Scotia but to those in all provinces affected. Other provinces, however, except in a sympathetic way, do not come within my purview. I must repeat that the vote of $300,000 for needy fishermen in all the provinces where fisheries are established is a useless sum, and cannot be effective. I was going to use a word which, though perhaps not unparliamentary, would have been harsh, and I have no desire to use harsh language, even when replying to the leader of the opposition, for whom I have great respect.
Without any desire to embarrass the Minister of Fisheries but rather to help him I should like to know whether this is the final vote for needy fishermen throughout Canada. If the amount is divided it will be found that the needy fishermen in Nova Scotia cannot exist upon the amount which would go to them. I may be wrong, but it is my impression that in the Canadian west we have the wheat board and the wheat exchange. The price of wheat is fixed, and the government pays the difference between the market price and .the price which is fixed. On the other hand the fisherman must go his weary way upon the seas. He receives nothing from anybody, and he must sell for two cents per pound fish which is sold in stores for fifteen or sixteen cents per pound. Who receives the profit? The fishermen and the farmers are the backbone of Canada, and although the fish in the sea cannot be seen, as is the wheat grown on the western prairies, that is no reason why the fish should be forgotten. I can see no sound reason why a supplementary vote, one which would meet the requirements of fishermen, should not be brought down. The minister could stand behind it. These are days when general relief measures are necessary, but only the fishermen who go to sea, many of whom are going out for the last time, know the hardships of working night and day in cold fMr. Finn.]
weather, away from their families and their home districts.
These are the conditions which have caused me to speak forcefully this afternoon. I have no desire to embarrass the Minister of Fisheries, because this is the first year he has held office as minister of that department, but I believe it my duty to draw to his attention the needs and requirements of fishermen. Before the vote is passed I suggest some person or persons should be sent to find out the needs of the fishermen, how they live and what agreements have been entered into with the provincial governments. So far as my province is concerned I say that they should find out what agreement has been entered into with the government of the Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, Premier of Nova Scotia. Until that information is forthcoming I suggest that the minister should allow the item to stand to permit personal conferences with him, and he should be assured that before the item appears in the estimates careful study has been given to the whole matter, and that there is an understanding of conditions existing.
The hon. member for Gloucester spoke of legislation passed in 1935, and although I have tried to find out, I must say that I do not know to which particular act he refers. There is one which has reference to fisheries, another referring to relief and a third respecting people receiving titles, but I cannot see anything applying to fishermen.
