Mr. THOMAS REID (New Westminster) moved the second reading of Bill No. 20, to amend the Fisheries Act, 1932.

Fisheries Act-Mr. Reid
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset, may I say that the bill which I am introducing to the house is practically the same bill as was introduced last year. As this is almost a new house as far as members are concerned, perhaps it might be well if I stated briefly the objects of this bill. I shall endeavour to be as brief as possible, realizing, however, that some explanation is necessary. The proposed bill deals particularly with the salmon industry as related to the Fraser river. The Fraser river flows into the gulf of Georgia and its fresh waters carry out quite a few miles into the gulf. From confederation to 1933 the gulf of Georgia, the estuary of the Fraser river, has been fished entirely by those using gill nets.
So that hon. members may have a better idea as to what the dispute is about, I should explain that two methods are used principally in fishing for salmon in British Columbia. One method is the gill net operated by a fisherman, sometimes assisted by a helper but mostly working alone from his boat. The gill net is some 1,200 feet long by thirty feet deep. I am using the measurement of feet to describe these nets although the term "fathom" is used in the Fisheries Act.. I lelieve the expression "feet" will be more easily understood by the members. From confederation to 1933 only gill netters were permitted to catch fish in this area.
The other method of fishing is by seine nets. The seine boats carry a crew of from seven to nine men who go out into the open waters or clear salt waters when a school of fish is sighted, and may I say that a school of salmon is very easily located by the numerous sea-gulls and other birds hovering round. When a school of fish is sighted these seine boats drop their nets which measure 1,200 feet by some seventy-three feet, as against the thirty foot depth of the gill nets. They circle the school of salmon and then pull the net tightly together at the bottom with cords when it comes up like a purse. That is why they are called purse seines. The catch of fish made at one set by these nets is almost unbelievable. They have been known to pick up as many as 10,000 salmon at one lift. In fishing for herring they have been known to bring up as many as twenty-six tons at one time. Hon. members will readily understand the havoc wrought in a school of salmon by this type of fishing.
For the information of hon. members, may I point out that the salmon head through the straits of Juan de Fuca coming up from the southern Pacific ocean. They head also into t.he rivers of the Pacific coast, but principally
into the Fraser river. As I pointed out, seine fishing has been permitted in other areas, but this area was exclusive to gill netters from confederation to 1933. In 1922 a commission, consisting of many hon. members of parliament, some of whom are still in the house, was appointed to go to British Columbia to investigate the whole industry. This commission reported that in all areas where gill net fishermen could operate, seine boats should be prohibited entirely. It was felt that if seine fishing were allowed in certain areas the fishing industry would be depleted, due to the scooping up in large numbers of all varieties of fish, including immature fish. The mesh of the seine net is only three and one-quarter inches and when it is pulled tight, everything encircled within it is brought up.

They put some back into the sea.
_ Mr. REID: No, sir. I shall deal with that in a little while. As interjected by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), it is claimed that some fish are put back into the sea. This is the claim of the canneiy men, the principal owners of the seine boats, and the seiners themselves. I -have letters stating that immature fish and fish out of season have been sold in various Pacific coast cities after having been caught in these seine nets.
In 1933, when the house was in session, an order in council was passed permitting seine boats to go into this special area. This was done even though there was a standing fisheries committee. These seine netters had been besieging every government for many years to allow them to enter this area to fish. Contrary to the statement of the deputy minister of fisheries and others, seine boats are ninety per cent owned and controlled by the canning interests. They are really mobile traps because they can fish one area and then move on into another, and this is what has been taking place. The very day this order in council was passed I received from the acting Minister of Fisheries a letter, a copy of which I have in my hand, stating that this matter would be considered. This statement was made in that letter even though he or some one had signed the order in council that very day allowing seine boats to enter this area.
Mr. Speaker, at this point may I say I am particularly pleased at the appointment of a Minister of Fisheries. In 1930 there was a minister of fisheries and at that time I expressed my thanks. I was sorry to see the then Minister of Fisheries transferred, but from then until the elections we have had only an acting Minister of Fisheries. As
Fisheries Act-Mr. Reid

the first acting Minister of Fisheries, (Mr. Duranleau), pointed out to me, there was no use in his interesting himself in the fishing industry as he was only the acting minister. He left everything to the officials of the department. I am glad that a Minister of Fisheries has been appointed now because the fishing industry is one of the important industries of Canada.
I should like to direct attention to the fact that the value of the production of this industry has been going down from year to year. I shall not weary the house with figures, but in 1929 the value of the production of this industry was S53,518,521, the value of the British Columbia production being $23,930,602. In 1934-35 the production dropped to a total value of $34,121,941, the production in British Columbia having dropped to $15,334,335.
Was the first year 1929?
Yes.
Why not take a year comparable with 1935?
What year does the right hon. gentleman suggest?
Either 1932 or 1931.

In 1930 the total value was $47,804,216; in 1933-34 it was $27,558,053. If one takes the figures for successive years, it will be found that the total valuation drops from year to year. The increase in 1933 is due to the fact that there was an extraordinary run of certain variety of fish in that year. If I had the time to go into the figures, I could show a drop in quantity and in value from year to year. Salmon fishing is the most important fishing industry in British Columbia. Out of a total of production last year amounting to $15,334,335, the value of the salmon industry was $12,351,641. It is practically the greatest industry we have in British Columbia.

Except lumbering and
mining.

I was speaking particularly
of this variety of fish as against others. In 1933 there was invested in vessels practically $25,000,000 and in canneries $16,000,000, or a total of $41,000,000, and in 1934-35 that total was over $43,000,000. In 1933 there were employed 65,391 persons and in 1934-35 that number had increased to 68,634. The total number of those employed in the industry including those on shore was last year 82,372. The number of those engaged in fishing had increased, for the reason no doubt that many who had prior to that time been unemployed 
went into the fishing business in an effort to obtain a livelihood. This, I believe, dhows the importance of the industry.
The dispute in question affects the livelihood of some 2,000 fishermen, and I have already painted out that this area had been fished exclusively by gill nets. With reference to orders in council, the 1922 commission recommended that adequate notice should be given before the passing of any orders in council, and in this connection I would direct the attention of the house to a matter which I consider serious. We seem to be drifting into this position: We pass the nucleus of a law and then allow the minister or his department to issue large booklets of regulations which practically change the whole act. I hold in my hand the latest orders in council passed this year and together they are almost as copious as the act itself. They were passed without any information having been previously given out, although the statement is made that the matter had been discussed with the industry. Here we have orders in council passed almost as bulky as the act itself, and this done practically without the sanction of parliament. I wish to call the -minister's attention to a particular clause, and I would ask the house whether it is not something unprecedented as far as orders in council are concerned. I am referring to the regulations having to do with the inspection of canned salmon.
The documents to which the hon. gentleman is referring include regulations as well as orders in council.

Perhaps they do, but wait
until you hear this one.

The order in council is
passed to validate the regulations.
-Mr. REID:	The documents I have before
me include orders in council and regulations; I say that so that the minister and I shall be in agreement. Regulations have been passed in connection with canned salmon, for both export and import. In connection with canned salmon coming into Canada, -this is what section 32 (b) says:
All shipments of canned salmon imported for sale in Canada shall enter through a British Columbia port only.
Can the house imagine a provision that all potatoes entering Canada shall come in through Prince Edward Island or Nova Scotia, or that all strawberries shall enter through Ontario? I do not know whether -the minister has seen this provision, but it seems to me-

Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to read that again.

Fisheries Act-Mr. Reid
32(b). All shipments of canned salmon imported for sale in Canada shall enter through a British Columbia port only.

It is not worth the
paper it is written on.

As a layman, I say the same,
and I doubt whether it was called to the attention of the minister. But it shows what is happening to-day. Regulations are drawn up and if they are passed while the house is sitting no minister has time to look at them; naturally the minister takes the word of the deputy or of the departmental officials. And this is just a sample of what we have been getting. It is preposterous and I hope the minister will look carefully into it. I hold that it had been the policy of the Liberal government that no purse seine fishing should be allowed in the area conserved. The commission that sat in 1922 went into the matter thoroughly and submitted its findings, which were adopted by the house. I could put on the record statements to show that an assurance was practically given the fishermen by the present Prime Minister last year that something would be done to conform with the recommendations of the report of the commission that investigated the matter in 1922. I think I could say there was almost a promise that this would be done. The seines were first allowed in on the argument that the question was one of quality. It was said that as United States fishermen were fishing with seine boats and were also using traps, the fish, which the acting minister had been told were out in this area, deteriorated, when they crossed into Canadian waters. Well, I could read affidavit after affidavit from men who have fished there for twenty-five or thirty years, to the effect that in all their experience over the past thirty years there was a greater catch of salmon from the area by gill nets. As to the question of quality, the waters of the Fraser river flow out many miles, and any one crossing either by boat or by aeroplane can see the line of demarcation where the salt water meets the fresh water of the Fraser river. The argument in regard to quality is an erroneous one. For instance, in 1934 the area was closed for two weeks and the supervisor informed the public and the fishermen that the fish at that time were not in a fit state to be canned; that they had so deteriorated. But then he allowed the area to be opened up again and fishing took place by both seine and gill nets and the fish caught were canned.
Did he intimate that the closing for twelve days was on account of quality?

If the closing of the area had anything to do with the question of quality he would not have allowed fishing two weeks after the fish had had time to deteriorate still more. I suggest to the minister that it is not always a question of locality; it is very often a question of time. I do not know whether the deputy minister has ever had the fish timed to see how long it takes them to come from the international boundary to the Fraser river. At any rate, the argument was that the seine boats should be allowed to catch the fish in this area, because, if the fish were allowed to come up they would be in such bad condition as to ruin the good name of our sockeye. And here I might point out the late run of sockeye is not exactly the same as the early, and the inspection act, in my opinion at any rate, was introduced primarily with the idea of allowing the seine boats to get into this area, because the canners argued that it was a question of quality and they wanted to take the fish early so as to get a first-class product; at least so they stated. When the canners in the United States can the same variety, the late run of sockeye, they market the fish not as sockeye salmon but as "reds," because the late run of sockeye has a red skin and the belly is white, being different from the early run of sockeye which made the name of Fraser river, British Columbia, famous. I say this in all seriousness to the minister: If notice is not taken of this the canners, by canning this late run of sockeye and labelling it and selling it in the markets of the world as No. 1 sockeye, will do more damage to the good name of sockeye than anything else I know of. I ask that he take particular note of this and investigate to see whether what I say is not correct, and also that the United States, in putting up the same fish, label it as "reds," not as sockeye.
Would section 98 apply?

I do not know, of course, but I think section 98 would apply to some of the arguments put up by certain of the canners. They catch immature fish and destroy it, and I can support my assertions with numerous letters. I also have before me the argument advanced by the United States. In a letter which I received last year from the department of fisheries, Seattle, Washington, it is stated, "We have ruled purse seines out of the latter district and off the
Fisheries Act-Mr. Reid

coast of Washington within our jurisdiction to prevent the catching of immature fish." I cite that to show that United States interests have at last recognized that the seines are destructive in that they catch immature fish as well as all other varieties. As I pointed out, the size of the mesh is only three and one-quarter inches to begin with, and when pulled tight it is not over one and a half inches and becomes virtually a trap. I wonder whether any members of the house have seen the fish being taken from the seines. At one period last year they had so many fish, caught by seines, lying on the wharves, that when the canneryman got to the bottom of the seine, the flesh of the fish on the bottom fell away from the bones; they were as bad as that. Some say that fish caught by seines are of better quality than those caught by gill nets, but they are not. I am sorry that I have not an opportunity to develop that angle of the matter further, much as I would like to.
Is the purse seine used on the American side?

Purse seines are used on the American side but not at the mouths of rivers. They have ruled them off the Columbia and other rivers. There is a conflict of opinion in the United States the same as we have in Canada, perhaps to a greater extent, in that there are state regulations and federal regulations which often come into conflict. But the state has ruled out seines from the mouths of rivers.
From the mouth of the Fraser river?

They do not fish at the mouth of the Fraser river. The minister means the Canadian seines? The American seines are barred by the boundary line, but Canadian seiners, when they had the chance, have seined right up into the Fraser river. As I mentioned in committee last year, three or four of them were caught right up in the river in shallow water.
When I introduced this to the committee last year I lost by one vote; eight voted against me while seven voted for the bill, and the chairman of that fisheries committee told me that had the vote been eight to eight he would have given his casting vote in my favour. I accept that in good faith; he told , me that without my having to ask him about it. But I would point out that I lost out in the committee by only one vote. I stated when the matter came into the house, and I am going to state again, that the officials of the fisheries department gave misleading

information, and have done right along, in regard to the salmon fisheries. I know that it is considered quite a crime to mention any official in this house, because the official is not here, but I mentioned the matter in front of him, and I contend that when there is anything wrong it is the right of the member to rise in his place and complain, so long as he is not vindictive in doing so. When he finds that wrong information has been supplied to the minister it is the member's duty, as I see it, to say so in this house. I repeat that departmental officials have certainly given misleading information right along.
I have not time to go into all the arguments used by the deputy minister last year, but I say that about twenty-five per cent of the statements which were made were open to disputation and at least fifteen per cent of them were entirely wrong, could not be proved. He said that fifty per cent of the seines were owned by the canneries. He did not say that ninety per cent were owned and controlled; he said that fifty per cent were owned. The information given me in British Columbia is that at least ninety per cent of the seines are controlled and owned by the canneries. He stated that the United States got most of the fish. Well, they may do so in some years, but, as I showed at that time, not in all years. He said that there were no purse seines permitted for sockeye. It is true that there were no purse seines for sockeye, but the canneries wish to have them, and in their briefs last year to the minister and to the committee they advocated the opening up of the area for them to fish when and how they liked. He stated that the dealers were reserving their best label for Canadian goods. I pointed out the racket that was played off last year, and I think is being played off this year: That canned fish had been inspected and classified as second quality; that, as our regulations required, another lid was put on the fish, and that fish was sold to customers who flicked off the first lid after the shipment left the shores of this country and sold the fish in their own markets as No.
1.	Some firms had also the temerity to ask for a rebate for taking off those lids. Now they are compelled to put on a lid that is soldered in four points, and what do you think has happened? There are firms offering to take off the soldered lids at so much per case, without leaving any mark; they do it by heating, and the second lid drops off and leaves the can intact. That fish is going to Great Britain and entering into competition with what we believe is No. 1 fish. Then the deputy minister said that the United States could pay more because of their home market.

Fisheries Act-Mr. Reid
The United States pays far more to the fisherman for catching the fish then we do in British Columbia; yet they sell the product for one-half the price to the United States consumer. I produced in this house cans of fish bought here and also bought across the line at just half the price. When the canneries were paying the fishermen one cent for late-run sockeye the United States paid ten cents and took the fish across the line and canned them, and those fish, which were not acceptable to our canners, were canned across the line and, I suppose, will meet our fish in competition in world markets.
I say without fear of successful contradiction that the present fisheries set-up is opposed absolutely to the gill net fisherman. The slant it has on life is all for the canner and for the vested interests. I say that after at least six years' investigation. In the arguments presented before the committee not one good word was said by the deputy in favour of the gill net fishermen. Every word that was spoken was in favour of the canner and, as I say, of the vested interests. I realize that once the department takes a stand it has to adhere to it. It cannot very well back down. I am pleased that we have now a full-time minister. I ask him not to take too seriously all the statements made by his departmental officials until he has had time personally to go out to British Columbia and investigate for himself. When he does investigate, for heaven's sake let him leave some of his officials behind and go out with some of the fishermen, and he will get an entirely different picture, whereas if he goes out with his officials they will show him the things which they want to show him and which, of course, will bolster up the stand they have long adopted, against the gill net fisherman.
I have pointed out that the fisheries will be depleted by the seine going in. I have figures to show that the catch has decreased since they went in. White springs, red springs and other varieties have been dropping off since these mobile traps have gone in. If the mobile traps could catch the fish more cheaply or of better quality I would say that there might be something to it, but in these days when we are looking for work for men and when we are talking about machinery displacing men, why should we allow these mobile traps, controlled by the vested interests, to put two thousand fishermen out of business? It is no wonder that I feel very wrathy about this matter.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before I close, I have three, if not four very important matters to bring to the attention of hon. members, and
particularly to the attention of the minister. I would like to have had my resolution in connection with the sockeye salmon treaty come before the house so that I could have dealt with this question more fully. I cannot go into this extensively to-night because I have not the time, but I would ask the minister to examine the map in connection with that sockeye treaty and see if he thinks his officials were right in laying out the boundaries. It is well known that south of the line the Columbia river contains all kinds of fish, and also that United States fishermen have caught fish out in the open sea in and out of season. But if the minister looks at the map he will see what poor information his officials must have had to O.K. a plan of that kind. We signed the treaty in 1930; it has not been signed by the United States yet. If they do sign it I hope the minister will not have departmental officials act as commissioners; I hope he will look after the fishermen and put on that commission someone who really knows and understands the fishing industry and who is really representative of the fishermen.
In connection with the late sockeye I have pointed out what I claim is the difference between the late and the early run. These sockeye are permitted to be canned and put on the market in competition with the No. 1 sockeye, and if this continues it will certainly ruin the valuable market we have built up for No. 1 sockeye.
Now I come to another matter. Last year I placed on the order paper a question which the then Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated was a matter of first rate international concern. I refer to something that has taken place in connection with the Columbia river, which at one time was a great salmon river. In that connection may I point out that away back in 1846 there was signed between Great Britain and the United States, a treaty, one clause of which reads as follows:
From the point at which the 49th parallel of north latitude shall be found to intersect the great northern branch of the Columbia river, the navigation of the said branch shall be free and open to the Hudson's Bay Company, and to all British subjects trading with the same, to the point where the said branch meets the main stream of the Columbia, and thence down the said main stream to the ocean, with free access into and through the said river or rivers; it being understood, that all the usual portages along the line thus described, shall in like manner be free and open.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, after 1846 the Columbia river, by treaty, was to be kept open for Canadian and British subjects, but during the past number of years the
Fisheries Act-Mr. Reid

United States have ignored that treaty entirely and have built large dams and other obstructions. One dam, I think, is some 370 feet in height, so that to-day there can be no portages. In addition this has affected the runs of fish in that river. I have in my hand the annual bulletin of the Department of Fisheries of the state of Washington, which says:
Practically all of the Columbia river watershed in eastern Washington has been drained of its fish life almost to the point of extermination because no support was given by the public to enforcing legislation already on the statute books.
We have the same situation on tJhis side of the line; we have complacently stood by while the United States have openly violated this treaty. That clause in that treaty was of untold value to Canada; I do not know that I could state the amount in money that it was worth to the people of this country. New that river is blocked. I appeal to the Minister of Fisheries and to the Prime Minister to take up this matter very seriously with the United States government. I do not know what can be done about it now, or what compensation we should demand, but I do know that if conditions had been reversed and we had done this, the United States would have made us pay heavily for blocking that river. A part of that treaty has been ignored, and no notice has been taken of it. As a quid pro quo I would suggest that we be given a small piece of land adjacent to Vancouver, a small neck of the woods called Point Roberts, which is United States territory at the present time. At times this has been more or less of a bootlegging centre, though in the summer time it is a great summer resort, and customs officials are maintained there. We who are acquainted with the district know exactly what is going on there. I say it would not be too much to ask that the United States transfer this small piece of territory to Canada in compensation for the violation of the treaty of 1846. No one can say just when that portage might have been of benefit to this country; no one can say when in future it might be desirable to use it, but now it is blocked, and I say it is too bad that no action has been taken by the Canadian government. As I said, I took up the matter last year and it was pointed out by the then Prime Minister that this was an international question.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I am not asking for the total elimination of seines. I am asking that they be eliminated from the mouth of the Fraser river, where they were allowed to be placed in 1933 for

the first time. They 'have other areas available, and when those areas are closed they can move to other areas such as Nos. 18, 19 and 20. The gill nets cannot go there because it is clear salt water and those of us who know anything at all about the fishing industry know that gill nets do not do so well where the water is clear, because the fish can see the nets and so avoid them. It is strange that in the regulations there should be indicated a maximum length and depth for gill nets, though when it comes to the seiner he can use a net of any length or depth he desires.
There is one more matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister, and that is with regard to the policy of his department in regard to propagating sport fish. I know that we want tourists to come to this country; I know they like our streams, but we have spent many thousands of dollars in the propagation of sport fish which, on investigation, have been found to prey upon the small salmon fry. In other words we have been spending money to develop a salmon fishing industry and at the same time we have been spending money to cultivate the enemies of the salmon fishing industry. Dolly Varden and other trout, from the mouths of rivers where the salmon fry were found, have been opened up, and some of them have been found to have as many as sixty-five small salmon fry inside them. That is not bad for one meal, I would say. If you multiply that by the number of sport fish in our salmon streams you will see that this means a great loss to our fisheries, and I would ask the minister to take note of this situation. Sport fish may be all very well in many rivers, but I claim that in the salmon river the government should take note of what these sport fish are doing in the way of eating up the small salmon fry.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I understand that out of the money appropriated this year the minister is going to spend a certain amount in an attempt to encourage, by way of advertising, the consumption of fish. It appears to me that the greatest obstacle to the consumption of fish in this country, especially throughout the prairies and in the eastern provinces, is the price due to cost of transportation, et cetera. Remember that fishermen get about a cent and a half for a whole fish and then look what one must pay for fish in the stores. If the minister would approach the railway companies or have some regulation by which fish would be hauled across the country at cheaper rates so as to allow the public to get it cheaper he would

Fisheries Act-Mr. Michaud
do more to popularize fish than by simply having some woman stand in a store and show the housewife, who perhaps knows more about cooking than she does herself, how to fry fish. That to my mind will never popularize to any extent fish as a food. Advertising is all very well, but it seems to me that the most effective way to popularize fish would be to have railway rates and postal rates reduced so that there would be a ready market for cheaper fish both on the prairies and in the interior of British Columbia. It is scandalous that a fishermen can get only one and one-half cents for a fish weighing ten or fifteen pounds. I know that idea will not meet the views of the canners; no, they want everyone to eat canned fish. But we can ship our good canned salmon abroad, and I say again: If they want the people to eat the canned salmon they should at least sell it as cheap as the people across the line can purchase it. That they can well afford to do.
Now the seines will not be on this year; 1936 is the off year, but notice should be given now that they will not be allowed in 1937. The livelihood of two thousand fishermen is affected. Not only that, but the seines, just mobile traps, are the most destructive form of fishing, and if they are allowed to continue, their large catches, coupled with the fact that they take everything in the net, immature fish and all, will certainly deplete our great salmon fisheries. In support of that I can point to other areas off the British Columbia coast which have been depleted by the use of seines and have had to be closed down to allow the fish a chance to propagate again.
I say in all seriousness that the department is against the fishermen. I want the minister to investigate why in 1934 they allowed the seine boats in twelve hours before the gill net fishermen. Thirty-five mobile traps went into that school of fish; some of them ten thousand fish at a clip, and there were dumped on the cannery wharves so many fish that they could not be canned. And yet the department talk about quality.
I wonder if hon. members know the kind of letter sent out by the department. This is a paragraph from a letter that was sent to every canner; I leave it to hon. members if this is fair:
I have been further requested to obtain from each cannery manager a communication setting out his opinion as to whether the seine caught fish were superior for canning purposes as compared to fish caught by means of gill nets-
A very leading question.
Who signed it?

Mr. McLeod, supervisor acting under the chief supervisor at Vancouver acting under the deputy minister at Ottawa. A leading question, meaning: Yes, we want you to say the seine caught fish are the best. How could they say otherwise when ninety per cent of these mobile traps are owned and controlled by the canners? Then they send out this letter to bolster up the order in council passed in 1933 which allowed these traps into that area.
I hope the minister will take these remarks seriously; this is a very serious matter; I introduced the bill last year and lost by one vote, so this year I am looking for results.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member must at least be congratulated upon having been able to tack on to his remarks about four different subjects which have no relation to the bill itself. However I have very little time at my disposal, so let me state briefly the position of the department and the government in relation to the matter. I shall proceed by way of elimination.
To take the last statement first, that in his opinion the Department of Fisheries is antagonistic to the fishermen; this statement is not warranted by .the facts and by the policy of the department for yearn past. I cannot and do not pretend to speak for my predecessors in office or to excuse whatever attitude or policy they may have adopted in reference to the matter of salmon fishing in British Columbia. However I may say in fairness to my predecessors, whom I have had the pleasure of knowing personally, that no sinister or ulterior motive actuated them in adopting the regulations of which my hon. friend complains. Since this bill was first introduced by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) I have made it my duty to look into the matter and to try to find out whether his attitude is justified.
As to his complaints relating to matters of international concern, such as the attitude this government or this country should take towards the United States of America regarding the Columbia river, and the line which was adopted by the contracting parties to the treaty of Washington, or the sockeye salmon treaty, which by the way I may say is in process of being revised or studied by both parties, these matters have no reference to the bill which is now under consideration, so for the present I shall eliminate any answer to these questions, which are intricate matters the reply to which might be far-reaching if I attempted at the present time to state the attitude of the government.

Fisheries Act-Mr. Michaud
My hon. friend also tried to confuse the. idea of quality or the policy of inspection with the regulations respecting seining at the mouth of the Fraser river. I find that the licensing of seiners in those waters came about as a consequence of the rules for inspection which were established in 1932 by the Department of Fisheries, and sanctioned by order in council of the government of the day. One matter which I want to explain, lest I should forget, is the complaint of my hon. friend about certain regulations of the department, especially one which he read, which has reference to the inspection of canned salmon when entering Canada. It is true that this regulation stands as it was read. But it is no new regulation, and it was adopted for a purpose. Practically all canned salmon that enters Canada comes through the Pacific coast, where in t'he United States practically all the salmon is canned. The regulation insists that salmon entering Canada from the United States should enter through entry ports in British Columbia, because it is only in that province that we have canned salmon inspection and inspectors. Inasmuch as most of the salmon enters Canada through the Pacific coast it is natural we should insist that it be inspected where we have inspectors.
As to the bill itself, it is in the nature of an injunction or prohibition. The hon. member seeks to have parliament prohibit the governor in council or the department exercising the function or prerogative which they have the duty to exercise under the existing law. The Fisheries Act provides that the governor in council on the recommendation of the minister may licence or sanction the mode of fishing, and these types of fishing have been accurately described by the hon. member.
Before 1933 the Department of Fisheries did not see fit to recommend to the government the approval of seine fishing in the waters lying at the mouth of the Fraser river in the gulf of Georgia, and in that year a regulation was adopted. Before stating the reasons which prompted the government to adopt the regulation I should like to take time to lay before the house certain facts and conditions which led the government of the day to determine upon the procedure of licensing that mode of fishing. It is true that prior to that year fishing with purse seines for salmon in those waters was not permitted. Hon. members coming from British Columbia know better than I do the conditions existing in the waters adjoining the province. For the information of hon. members who may not be familiar with the situation may I say that there are two kinds or two runs 
of sockeye salmon in the waters in question. Although t'he fact may be well known to all members, I should like to repeat that the Fraser river sockeye salmon is admitted by all the world to be the best obtainable for canning. When I make this statement I refer to the early run of fish. The early run is of grade A quality, and is found in those waters in the early season of the year and until about August 20 or 25. May I add that there is no regulation permitting the catch of that first-class fish by the use of seines. No purse seine fishing is permitted before the late run of fish appears in those waters, and through some freak of nature the late run fish appear only in odd years.
The first run of fish of the late variety is what is known as pink salmon. It is a good quality fish, but is not equal in quality to the genuine, early Fraser river sockeye. Then there is the late run sockeye which the hon. member claims is not a true sockeye. On that point I will not argue, as I am not familiar enough with conditions either to dispute the fact or to prove the contrary. However it is recognized by the trade as being an inferior grade of sockeye. It is permissible at certain times of the year to catch the late run of sockeye by seine fishing. Generally, from August 25 until the middle or latter part of September this kind of fishing is permitted due to the fact that since 1933 inspection has been in force in British Columbia. Before that time it could not be permitted, because the salmon was packed and when packed was put on the market as Fraser river sockeye. This procedure tended to depreciate the value, quality and good name of our good quality fish on the world market. However, after the rules for inspection were adopted in British Columbia, the government said to the canners:	It will be
up to you; wre have a means of deciding whether the fish you put on the market is good quality, second quality or an inferior grade, and if you choose to buy and can fish which will not grade properly it will be your misfortune, and you must suffer the consequences.
Purse seining was permitted because it was claimed-and the hon. membeT has not disputed the claim-that the fish caught in the cold waters immediately beyond the entrance to the mouth of the Fraser river, and just over the American border or boundary, is a good fish, of such quality that it can be put in cans, and when canned will appear as a good grade of fish to be placed on the market. That is the reason purse seining is allowed in those waters. The claim is made that gill net fishing cannot be done

Supply-Fisheries
as effectively as purse seining. Only a very small territory is in dispute, namely in the waters close to the imaginary line which forms the boundary between the United States and Canada, and the clear waters at the mouth of the Fraser river to which gill netters cannot resort.
We claim that if our fishermen can continue to catch late in August or early September fish of such quality or in such state that it can be packed satisfactorily, it would be in the interests of the fishermen to make the catch. By such permission they would be obtaining money which otherwise they would not receive. That is the reason why in 19'33 purse seining was permitted. Had the department thought this method of fishing would injuriously affect the trade in fish, I am sure my predecessors in office, no matter to which party they may have belonged, would not have allowed that mode of fishing. After all it would be bound to reflect upon all fishermen or other people engaged in the trade. The regulation is not made for the benefit of the eanners, directly, although it is true that they benefit by it. However, if they do benefit it is because the fishermen can catch the fish; the canner does not catch it.
The hon. member has tried to impute motives to officials of the department because they did not agree with him as to the ownership of seine boats. My reply is that departmental officials can only state facts. We know who own the seining boats by the number of people who are registered as owners. Perhaps the hon. member is in a better position than departmental officials to know who the controlling interests may be. I submit, however, that it is only a matter of surmise, and that it is not a certainty. Officials of the department may have found it impossible to establish exactly whether or not eanners have controlling interests in boats registered under the names of other persons. When departmental officials state that only fifty per cent of the boats engaged in seine net fishing are owned by the fishermen themselves, the statement is made because the registrations have so indicated.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.

When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing vote No. 314.
Other projects-to aid, in cooperation with provincial governments concerned, in reestablishment of needy fishermen, $300,000.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was speaking on the item to which you have just referred. During the dinner recess I had hoped to have an opportunity of discussing one or two matters with the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), to which I made reference this afternoon, but unfortunately I had an engagement of an impelling nature, although not absolutely necessary, which prevented my interviewing the minister. This item has to do with the reestablishment of needy fishermen and in order that hon. members may deal intelligently with this matter, I think they should know what arrangements have been entered into with the provincial governments in connection with the item. Another important piece of information which we should have is how much the provincial governments are contributing towards the fund for the needy fishermen referred to in this item. If the Minister of Fisheries is desirous of replying to these questions, I am prepared to take my seat so that the committee may have this information.
Go ahead.

The Minister of Fisheries tells me to go ahead, but sometimes it is pretty hard to go ahead when you have no fuel with which to travel. In this case the fuel is the information. I have absolutely no desire to embarrass the minister, but this information is necessary in order to discuss intelligently this item from the standpoint of the needy fishermen. I do not even know what provinces are included in these arrangements; I do not know whether they cover the fisheries of the great lakes or whether they apply only to the Atlantic coast, the St. Lawrence river and the far-away Pacific coast. If I had this information, with what I have here in connection with my own province I could make a sort of race track estimate of what the needy fishermen of Nova Scotia might expect to receive. Therefore I ask the minister to give this committee some information as an index of his policy, and, I assume, that of the government. Until I receive that it is impossible for me intelligently and adequately to discuss matters which concern the needy fishermen in my constituency and in the province of Nova Scotia.

Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) may I say that the agreements with the provinces concerned are not yet concluded although they are in process of negotiation. Naturally, the provinces concerned will be those over which the dominion government has jurisdiction in connection with fisheries



Supply-Fisneries
These will be Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, British Columbia and those sections of Quebec over which we still have some jurisdiction. The $300,000 has not been finally apportioned because the distribution will depend upon the schemes and proposals to be submitted by the respective provinces. As this is a measure of emergency, it is intended to ask the provinces to contribute a share towards taking care of these people. After all, these people are citizens of the provinces and the provinces should contribute. They will be asked to contribute at least fifty per cent of the cost of administering such schemes or proposals for relief as they may submit to this department. If the proposals submitted are considered to be for the reestablishment of needy fishermen, we will contribute fifty per cent of what the provinces may deem it advisable to expend for such purposes.
As I understand the minister, he has no undertaking from any province that they are prepared to pay fifty per cent of the amount contributed by the federal government. Am I right?

In some respects, yes. As yet there are no undertakings, but some of the provinces have signified their willingness to adopt certain schemes for the relief of needy fishermen, to which schemes .the government will contribute. I understand that four of the provinces have signified their intention of going ahead and that within the next few days they will submit projects or schemes which are now in the course of preparation. The premier of British Columbia has signified his desire to avail himself of the privilege of sharing in the amount, and so have the premiers of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. But the details of the proposal have not yet been submitted.
On a policy of insurance.

Yes, insured; you cannot insure the land. As the member for Gloucester says, they could come and seize the land.
The adoption of such a proposal would do a great deal to aid the bona fide fisherman. We would not be pauperizing him; we would be doing something for people who are will-
Supply-Fisheries

ing and able to help themselves; and I think it would assist in doing away with this idea that we have to give hand-outs to people, an idea which is abhorrent to the average decent fisherman of British Columbia and, I have no doubt, of the Atlantic coast also.
There are methods, which I would term of a general nature, by which we could help the men engaged in the industry to help themselves. I have before me a resolution which was passed by the Kyuquot Trollers Cooperative Association, a very useful, aggressive and thrifty organization that has built itself up, even in bad times, to a measure of success. The resolution, which is addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), states that the salmon trollers are all independent fishermen owning and operating their own boats, ninety per cent of which are propelled by gasoline engines, and fifty per cent of the fish is marketed in the United States, a duty of a cent and a half a pound being paid thereon. American fishermen trolling on the same ground three miles from the Canadian shore enter their fish free and pay only half as much for their gasoline. I think I 'have heard it calculated that gasoline costs amounts to forty per cent or more of the expenses of a man trolling, because the boat has to be run at a slow rate of speed, and the fisherman has to go out ten, twenty, or thirty miles, and back again at night. It is calculated that the cost of gas and dil amounts to nearly fifty per cent of his running cost, so that his costs are double those of his competitor. The fishermen are asking the Prime Minister if he cannot do something towards reducing the high price of gasoline. A reduction would help them substantially, and help them all. The other point they touched upon was the duty of a cent and a half which they had to pay for entry to the United States, which is the market for that great class of their fish which they call springs. We know that the government in the reciprocity treaty with the United States obtained a reduction from two cents to one and a half cents a pound, but I notice a cut was made in the eastern provinces on some fish from two cents to one cent, and we in the west are disappointed, wondering why the reduction of fifty per cent was not made for our benefit at the same time. If that could be done it would help our fishing materially, because the United States is our market for that class of fish.
After all, what is the greatest aid we can give to the fisherman? Is it not a bountiful supply of fish and a good market? Grant him those things, and he does not need a hand-out. Grant him a plentiful supply of
fMr. Neill.]
fish, and help to get a good market; he will do all the rest himself, and the government will not have to spend $300,000 on it, either.
There are a number of ways in which the fishermen can be helped. I am going to mention two or three. One is by the abolition of traps in the neighbourhood of southeastern Vancouver island. I hold in my hand a letter from the department stating, as plain as language can be, that these licences would not be issued next year, and yet in Hansard on March 9 an answer was given by the same department to the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Plunkett), in which reply the very opposite was stated. We have been keeping these traps on, and the only excuse for years and years was that on the American side they had traps. Two years ago t'he Americans took their traps off-it was a gesture, and a big one

and they invited us to do the same. We have not done it. We have said: There is yet one year to go, and perhaps they will change. Now another year has gone by; we have this division between the departmental deputy on one hand and the Hansard report on the other, and we do not know whether the traps will be taken off and not permitted again. That is one measure which would be of practical benefit, because all who are familiar with the subject know that the traps are the most disastrous way to take fish. They are, as the word indicates, practically a trap for everything that comes along; big and small fish of all kind go in there and are destroyed. In destructive capacity they are next to the seines, which are also a very destructive method of fishing, and much for the same reason, because they take in big and little fish as well.
Then we have the question of cutting down the hair seals. Here again I have a petition that was got up by a meeting of trollers on the Pacific coast last December. They made some comment upon the increasing number of hair seals. I took the matter up with the department, and I was advised on December 10 that the hair seal bounty was discontinued in June, 1933, owing to the need of strict economy in public expenditures. That was three years ago. Times now are a little better, and it is to be hoped that we can do a little something towards replacing that bounty. There is no more idiotic method of handling a bounty on any predatory animal or fish than doing it intermittently. If you take it off for two or three years the predatory animal or fish has time to recover. We tried that in British Columbia with cougars and wolves, and as a

Sup-ply-Fisheries
result there has been an enormous increase in the number of both those animals, because nobody is paid to hunt them. Indeed, instead of cutting down the bounty it should be increased, because it is more difficult to get them. I took the matter up with the department and the answer I got is this:
The department, however, is not in a position at the present time to say whether or not funds will be available for payment of the bounty next year.
That is entirely and thoroughly typical of .the correspondence I have with the department. "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep." Do not do anything but write a nice polite letter. Why do they not write me, if they are not in a position to speak definitely:	We will try
to see if we cannot get the bounty; we will look into the matter; we will take it up with the minister. But no, the department is not in a position to say, nor have they yet been able to say, whether funds will be available for payment of the bounty next year.
Take the allied subject of sea-lions. I have before me a resolution passed by a meeting of fishermen. I will not read the preamble. They say that fifty per cent of the fishermen's catches are at times second grade owing to the fish being mutilated by sea-lions. Apparently they play with the fish. They will catch a salmon, toss it in the air and catch it as it comes down. While watching sea-lions playing among themselves I have seen them doing this. The resolution asks if something cannot be done towards cutting down the numbers of these sea-lions. It has been the custom for a number of years to send one of the official patrol boats to the rookeries and destroy the sea-lions once a year. The patrol boats make the trip up to the Virgin islands, I think they are called. These fishermen ask if that practice cannot be extended, as the good effect of the sea-lions being caught is confined to one locality. These fishermen asked if that practice, which at present only affects one place, could not be extended lower down on the Pacific coast, to a place called Solander island near Cape Cook. These islands have been seen swarming with these sea-lions, which have proved detrimental to fishing operations. I took up. that question also, and after a good deal of correspondence the answer I received was that there was only enough money available to carry on the work at the Virgin rocks. I know that this work is done by one of the fishery patrol boats, the crew of which are paid all year. At that season they are simply cruising up and down the coast, and it would make hardly half a dollar's worth of difference whether they were cruising up and down under
steam or whether they went to this particular island, landed a crew and killed a number of these sea-lions at their breeding grounds. But this is the answer I received:
Some time ago arrangements were made to have the situation fully canvassed in view of the increasing complaints as to the depredations of the sea-lions upon the catches and gear of fishermen.
As you are aware, the funds available to the department for measures to control sea-lions in recent years are confined to the expenditure involved in the annual expedition to the Virgin and Pearl rocks off the entrances to Rivers and Smith inlets by means of the Givenchy.
The Givenchy is going up and down the coast all the time on patrol work. How much would it cost to land on these other rocks, right on the route, and put in a day hunting these sea-lions? I would be willing to pay for the ammunition myself, if that was all
that, was standing in the way. But that was____
what was the word used last year?-the laissez faire attitude of the department. Putting it into English, it means "let be,"' and no two words could better describe the policy of the department: Let be; leave eyerything alone; whatever is, is best; wait and see.
Then I took up another matter, not as an agitator wanting to make trouble for the department, but as a result of meetings of fishermen or as a result of petitions received from fishermen who found their means of livelihood materially interfered with. In this case it was a board of trade that brought up the matter, complaining of the number of blackfish in certain districts. They said that when the blackfish went up the gulf of Georgia it was impossible to catch salmon for two or three days afterwards; the tourists were disappointed and the tourist resorts lost customers, while the commercial fishermen lost trade also. I took up that matter with the department, from which I received a longish letter putting all sorts of obstacles in the way. In this case there was not one lion; there was a whole menagerie of lions in the way of having anything done. The department said:
Even to secure the carcasses of a few for the purpose of having an examination of the stomach contents made by bioligical officers
would present some difficulty____ In the light
of all the circumstances-
This is the summing up; this is the action for which a group of fishermen were waiting:
In the light of all the circumstances, it is proposed to see what arrangements are feasible tor securing a few specimens, preferably from the Discovery Passage area in the vicinity of Campbell river, with a view to having the stomachs analyzed to definitely determine, if possible, the food they eat.
Supply-Fisheries

That letter is dated December 30, but do not think progress has not been made. I received another letter dated February 26 in which I was told:
As previously advised, consideration is being given-
Do not be faint hearted!
-to arrangements for securing a few specimens of blackfish with a view to having their stomach contents analyzed to definitely determine, if possible, the food they eat.
They will get about half a dozen of these blackfish and look into their stomachs. If they happen to find seaweed they will say that the fish live on seaweed. I remember that on one occasion a man examined the stomach of a sea-lion on the Pacific coast. He found seaweed in the stomach and reported that the sea-lions lived on seaweed. Rubber tires are widely used on the fishing boats for fenders. If he had found a piece of rubber tire in the stomach of the sea-lion I suppose he would have reported that they lived on rubber. Supposing they took one of us at an odd moment and examined his stomach, what would be found? It would be that particular food we had last eaten. Supposing they get a blackfish and find no salmon in the stomach. That will not prove anything except that for a short time previously that blackfish had not been eating salmon. Maybe he was on a diet or something like that. But the best that I have been able to obtain, after all the correspondence which appears on this file, is that consideration is being given the matter. I am told not that something is going to be done, simply that consideration is being given to arrangements. Well, that will not help the fishermen much. Take some of your 8300,000 under this vote and use it to drive these blackfish out of the gulf of Georgia. This can be done; it was done before in connection with whales, and it will be of tremendous benefit to commercial fishermen and to those interested in the tourist business as well.
I made a reference to whales, and perhaps I might be allowed to explain what I meant. We can help also by clearing out log jams and such things which prevent the fish from going up at the right time to spawn. There are certain areas where, under certain conditions, the fish go up in large numbers at what is called high water. They go up and spawn on the banks of the rivers or creeks above the height of normal water. The result is that when the water subsides they are left high and dry; the frost comes along and enormous quantities of the spawn are destroyed. That could be prevented by netting those areas-they are principally government properties, rough bush-in such a way that the fish could not get beyond the ordinary water limit, compelling them to spawn within the area where they would be covered by water. I only hope that in his distribution of the largesse of which he has now been made the custodian he will use that measure of discretion which should characterize a minister seized with a sense of

his responsibility, notwithstanding what the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) has said.
It is highly edifying and interesting to hear the expressions of opinion made by a supporter of the administration regarding a new minister who has discharged his duties for only a few months. We can only wonder what the harvest will be for a longer period of time, as illustrated by the views taken by that independent member who sits to my right, but who always manages somehow to have the goodwill, shall I say, of the government at particular times when this is very useful. It appeared that the letters asked about were dated not December, 1934, as some had hoped they would be, but December, 1935, and February of the present year, which was somewhat of a shock to some of our friends who had expected that out of a sense of deep and abiding gratitude the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), to say nothing of the junior member for Halifax, would join together and make this attack upon the minister. This is at least interesting to us all and affords an opportunity to understand that, after all, there is beginning to be a realization on the part of the government that the administration in the days of stress and difficulty was not just as easy as it seemed to be when they were sitting on this side of the house. Responsibility has brought home to them a realization that it is much easier to sit to the left of the Speaker and to criticize than, sitting to his right, to provide the sinews of war on the one hand and the administration on the other.

I would like to correct a statement made by the right hon. leader of the opposition. He seems to be doing what I thought he would not do, that is grasping at a political straw. I made no criticism whatever of the hon. minister or of officials. I pointed out to the minister that I thought it was the duty of the department, himself and his officials, to look into this matter from every angle. I am not going to permit the leader of the opposition to put into my mouth his political words; I used my own, and Hansard will show them, and I would ask the right hon. gentleman to take that statement back.

Far be it from me to endeavour in my poor way to improve upon the elegant diction of the hon. gentleman. If I misconceived his observations as being criticism instead of commendation, then it may be that my understanding of the words "criticism" and "commendation" is not quite that of the hon. gentleman. If I have done
violence to his feelings or in any sense misunderstood him I can only say that it arises from the fact that I would have concluded that his observations constituted criticism and not commendation. Apparently I should have said that when I contemplate the commendation of the hon. junior member for Halifax of the activities of the Minister of Fisheries I am at a loss to understand what he would regard as criticism.

From the observations of the minister I take it that it is his intention to contribute on a fifty-fifty basis with the provinces; that if a province would contribute fifty per cent he would give fifty per cent of this fund to that province where needy fishermen are concerned. May I ask the minister what he is going to do in case a province does not provide anything as its part of the contribution?
It cannot share in the fund.

Therefore so far as this vote is concerned a province that does not cooperate and contribute cannot share in this fund.
The next item of course is not up for discussion. Something will depend upon that. The minister said a moment ago that this fund was intended to help fishermen who fish only part of the year; that there are fishermen who fish all the year round who would not share in this fund. That is a serious statement as far as I am concerned, because my fishermen fish all the year round, but nevertheless they find it difficult to make a living. If the fishermen who fish all the year round cannot share in this fund it is a serious matter for the fishermen in my constituency. Has the minister any observations to make in that regard? Will they come under the next item?
Indirectly they will, certainly.

In his genial way the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) severely criticized the officials of the Department of Fisheries. Although I have been connected with public affairs for many years, this is my first adventure in the House of Commons and so far as my constituency is concerned the fisheries officers are the officers who came to me when I was elected. By and large I consider them good officials. They are alert and I believe they are faithful in trying to do their work. I believe the same is true of the officers at Ottawa. I believe I can pick out a drone when I see one, and

I must say that while I have been round these offices quite a bit it is my belief that the officers of the department are trying to do their best. We must remember, however, that the Department of Fisheries is one dealing with prohibitions and regulations. How can we expect a department dealing with such matters to be popular with members of the House of Commons or with the people of Canada? The only money the Department of Fisheries ever had under its control was to be used for purposes of prohibiting something. There was nothing to sustain or develop fisheries. The Department of Fisheries is the Cinderella of the government, and it has been the Cinderella for many years. I think it is unfair to criticize unduly the officers of the department, and the only criticism I would make is that they should have been more aggressive with the treasury board, and should have seen to it that more money was voted for the development of fisheries in Canada.
In my province two kinds of fisheries are affected. My difficulty is not the same as that of the hon. members from British Columbia, because we have both fresh and salt fishing. The fresh fishing industry depends to a great degree upon the home market, while salt fishing depends upon the foreign market. In connection with our fresh fishing we are practically free of competition with the exception of that offered by Newfoundland at some periods of the year. We at least have the Canadian market for our fresh fish, and may I add at this point that the amount of fresh fish marketed in Canada has increased in the last five years.
According to the report of the price spreads commission 1929 was a big year in the fish industry, whereas 1932 and 1933 were small years. Since that time the fresh fish industry has been growing in Nova Scotia and in the maritime provinces generally. Notwithstand-i' g that fact, however, the fishermen cannot make a living. From the price spreads commission report we find that our fishermen earn from S75 to $300 per year. When I come to this House of Commons and hear hon. members talk about sustaining people on relief at $40 per month I have to smile, because our fishermen would live in comfort on $600 a year.
Why is it that our fishermen are not earning enough to keep body and soul together? The report of the price spreads commission tells the story. The reason is that the fisherman has lost his bargaining power. He must take what is offered him for his fish, and he is not able to have any say in what price the fMr. KinleyJ
product of his toil shall bring. Why is that so? One reason-and the minister knows it- is the steam trawler. We know that the steam trawler makes the corporation a primary producer. The trawler operator is put into the position where he can dictate prices to the fishermen of Canada. With his steam trawler he says in effect to the fishermen: "You will take what I want to give. If not, I have a steam trawler coming in to-morrow which will supply my requirements." To-night I am not going to discuss at length questions in connection with the steam trawler, but at some future time I shall do so.
If hon. members from other parts of Canada think we are against progress, then let them be at once undeceived, because the steam trawler people by their own figures admit that it costs them from one and a half cents to one and three-quarter cents to land a pound of fish. I have in my hand invoices from the National Fish Company at Halifax indicating that they paid one cent a pound on the average to a Nova Scotia fishing vessel for a trip before Christmas of this year. These men are working seventy hours at a stretch, are earning less than $8 a week and have families to support.
Parliament has spoken on the steam trawler question. The Maclean commission spoke on it and recommended against it. You may say, "Kinley, you are parochial in your viewpoint." That has been thrown in my face on many occasions. I say that my people are living in Canada, too, and it is not a criticism to say that something is done for them. If it is in favour of my people, then that should commend it especially when it is for the general good.
Doctor Cyrus Macmillan was not parochial. He was a member of the Duncan commission and was afterwards a member of the Maclean commission. Doctor Cyrus Macmillan in dramatic language and in no uncertain terms said that conditions were such that steam trawlers must be abolished, if fishermen were going to live. Then, in Nova Scotia there was set-up the Jones commission, presided over by Professor Jones of England. Connected with the commission were Mr. Alexander Johnston, the late deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and Doctor Innis of Toronto university. Were these men parochial? Alexander Johnston and Doctor Innis said that the steam trawler must be abolished if the fishermen of Canada are to be sustained or preserved.
Then we come to the price spreads commission of last year. Hon. members of this chamber served on the commission, and in their considered report what do they say?

They say that the fisherman has lost his bargaining power, and in order that he may get along the steam trawler must be gradually abolished in this country.
